description: Deep Space AI is a team of developers from Dushanbe, Tajikistan. We build AI-powered solutions with NASA open data: full-stack web, React/Next.js, Python, data analysis and machine learning.
summary:
FireChronicle is a web app that turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire detections into one consistent burning-activity calendar for any area in Central Asia, from November 2000 to today.

MODIS has recorded fires since 2000, but Terra and Aqua begin shutting down in late 2026–2027, and Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026. VIIRS continues the record at 375 m and reports about 3.5 times as many detections for the same fires. Stitching the sensors naively says Central Asia's fire activity rose 70% after 2012. In reality it fell by more than half (−51% for MODIS alone). The naive record gets the sign of the change wrong.

FireChronicle calibrates every VIIRS satellite (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) against MODIS, by country and month and with an orbit-drift term. It then combines all available sensors into one MODIS-equivalent estimate. As an independent check, monthly MODIS totals for years left out of calibration are predicted from VIIRS alone with R² 0.988, against 0.50 for a seasonal baseline.

Pick a country, draw an area or enter coordinates to see the calendar, how this month compares with the same days of past years, high-activity months ahead, anomalies and a 26-year 3D replay. You can then download CSVs or a briefing card. The data refresh daily from NASA FIRMS, so when MODIS goes dark the record continues on the same scale.
details:
What it does

FireChronicle answers the questions an emergency manager, land manager or scientist asks about an area: When is the fire season here? Is this month unusual? Which years were worst? Is fire activity changing? It answers them on a record that stays consistent across the change of satellites.

• Overview dashboard: the first screen an emergency manager sees.

• Sensor status: MODIS retiring, S-NPP ended, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 active.

• KPI tiles: last 7 days, this month and year to date, each vs normal; season status; active cells.

• "Last 24 months vs normal" with the P10–P90 band.

• A sortable country table and a ranked "where is it unusual now" list.

• Sections: Map, Calendar, Outlook, Anomalies, Compare, and Data & Method.

• Burning activity calendar: year × month, 2000–2026, on an accessible cividis colour ramp. Modes: harmonized, raw MODIS, raw VIIRS, naive splice, and a swipe that shows the naive and harmonized versions side by side.

• Live satellites layer: current positions of Terra, Aqua, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 from CelesTrak orbital elements (SGP4), with instrument swaths and "next passes over this area" in local time. It shows when the next detections can arrive.

• This month vs history: compares the current month so far with the same days of every past year (percentile and change vs median).

• High-activity months ahead: a 12-month climatological outlook from the last 10 years, labelled clearly as not a forecast, with a hindcast that checks how often it was right.

• Anomaly now: a map mode that ranks where the latest month is unusual compared with each cell's own history.

• Areas: country, drawn polygon, or point + radius. Two areas can be compared side by side.

• 3D map: time-lapse replay of 26 years, a fullscreen mode with glass panels, and five base maps. These include NASA GIBS true-colour imagery for the selected month, shaded relief and Black Marble night lights.

• Downloads: hotspot CSV for the area and dates, monthly series CSV, the full harmonized dataset, chart PNGs, a 1200×630 briefing card for messengers, and a citation.

• Ember, the SI (Super Intelligence) assistant: it answers only from a curated knowledge base (NASA FIRMS documents plus live FireChronicle numbers), using retrieval with exact-identifier priority. Every number in an answer is checked against its sources, off-topic questions are refused without calling a model, and charts in its briefing cards are drawn from our own data, never by the model. It replies in the language of the question (English, Russian or Tajik). Validated on a 33-question golden set: 100% retrieval hit rate, 100% honest refusals, 0 false refusals.

• Freshness: data are refreshed daily from NASA FIRMS. The page shows the last update, a countdown to the next one, and warnings if data become stale.

How it works

1. Data: NASA FIRMS standard-processing archives (MODIS C6.1; VIIRS 375 m S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), with near-real-time data for the latest months, marked provisional. That is 6.3 million raw rows for six countries (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan).

2. Cleaning: vegetation fires only (FIRMS type 0); MODIS confidence ≥ 30; VIIRS nominal or high confidence; persistent industrial sources removed with a fine H3 mask. That leaves 3.93 million detections.

3. Grid: H3 resolution 5 (~253 km²), counted monthly per sensor.

4. Calibration: each VIIRS satellite overlaps MODIS, so we fit the ratio VIIRS/MODIS per country × calendar month (Poisson maximum likelihood, shrunk toward the overall ratio). We add a yearly drift term because Terra and Aqua orbits are drifting (+1.1%/yr for S-NPP). Only science-quality years are used.

5. Harmonized value: the pooled minimum-variance estimate (M + ΣV) / (w_MODIS + Σk), weighted by how much of the month each sensor observed. It works before Aqua existed (Terra-only, 2000–2002) and after any satellite stops (S-NPP since 2 Nov 2026; Terra and Aqua when they shut down).

6. Uncertainty: an approximate 90% band from a bootstrap over calibration years, the 6.2% year-level calibration error, and Poisson counting noise.

7. Validation: leave-one-year-out prediction of monthly MODIS totals from VIIRS alone gives S-NPP R² 0.988 with bias −0.06%, NOAA-20 R² 0.976 and NOAA-21 R² 0.986, against 0.50–0.60 for a seasonal-climatology baseline. A Pettitt change-point test puts the naive splice break at the March 2012 sensor switch, while the harmonized and MODIS-only series break at January 2011, a real decline. Theil–Sen trend of annual totals: naive +534 detections/yr, harmonized −3,248/yr, MODIS alone −3,020/yr.

Benefits and intended impact

• A consistent fire history lets fire services in Central Asia plan for the months that matter and spot unusual activity early. It also lets them hand over a record that will survive the end of MODIS.

• Scientists get an open, reproducible harmonized dataset with uncertainty and a documented method.

• The method is general. It works for any region where FIRMS has data.

What makes it creative

• It is built around the satellite transition happening right now: Suomi NPP went dark 12 days before the hackathon.

• It shows the failure mode first: naive stitching flips the sign of the change.

• It uses NASA's own imagery (GIBS) as a basemap synced to the month you inspect, and shows live satellite passes.

• It is honest about uncertainty and limits.

• It refreshes itself daily.

Tools

• Pipeline: Python (Polars, NumPy, H3, Shapely, pytest).

• Web: TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, h3-js, Apache ECharts, satellite.js.

• Hosting: static site on GitHub Pages; daily refresh by GitHub Actions.

• SI assistant: a Cloudflare Worker with the Gemini API.

• Tests: 9 pipeline tests, 140 web tests and 54 assistant tests; the pipeline and web suites run on Linux in CI.

• Code (open source, MIT): https://github.com/komilovsg/firechronicle

What we considered

• A hotspot count is not burned area or fire size.

• Clouds and smoke hide fires.

• Near-real-time months are provisional.

• Calibration ratios after 2025 are held at their 2025 level.

• A high-activity month is climatology, not a forecast.

• Code is frozen at submission (tag v1.0-submission); only data refresh afterwards.

Use of SI (Super Intelligence) and automatic updates

• Ember is an SI assistant built on Google Gemini models (Gemini API, called from our Cloudflare Worker; the API key never reaches the browser). Its answers are marked "SI-written" in the chat. It answers only from our curated knowledge base and the live FireChronicle data, and every number it gives is checked against those sources.

• SI tools also helped the team with research, data analysis, coding, writing and the demo slides. Every number we publish comes from our pipeline and is covered by tests.

• Automatic updates: a GitHub Actions job pulls new NASA FIRMS data every day (with a second backup run), re-harmonizes it, runs the tests and redeploys the site. It is scheduled for six months, until 15 May 2027. After that it switches itself off and the last dataset stays online. The page shows the date and status of the latest update.

Next steps
• Alerts for fire services via Telegram or email and push notifications in a mobile app, so the right agencies hear about unusual burning in their district in time.
• An open API that delivers the harmonized data to other systems that need it.
